alexander-iii-stater-athena-and-nike-ale.note: Alexander kept his father's coinage of gold and silver and struck it at dozens of mints from Greece to Babylon, one of the largest coinages of antiquity. Athena wears the crested Corinthian helmet of Corinth's coins, a nod to the League of Corinth, the alliance of Greek cities that followed Philip and then Alexander against Persia. On the back Nike holds out a victor's wreath and carries a stylis, the mast-post of a warship and a sign of victory at sea: perhaps Salamis, perhaps Alexander's capture of Tyre in 332 BC. After his death in 323 BC his generals and the Greek cities went on striking the stater in his name for generations, so most are posthumous; the small symbols and monograms in the field tell the mints and dates apart.

philip-ii-stater-apollo-and-racing-chari.note: Philip II made Macedon rich with the gold of Mount Pangaion. He refounded the mining town of Krenides as Philippi in 356 BC, and the Greek historian Diodorus says its mines then yielded more than a thousand talents a year. From that gold came the staters the Greeks called philippeioi. Apollo, the god of Delphi, is on the front; on the back a charioteer races a two-horse chariot, a boast of Philip's wins in the horse races at Olympia (356, 352 and 348 BC). Delphi and Olympia belonged to every Greek, which made it a coin for all Greece. Alexander and Philip III kept striking it, and Celtic peoples copied it for some three centuries, the head and chariot slowly breaking up into the abstract patterns of Gaulish and early British gold.

lampsakos-stater-forepart-of-winged-hors.note: Lampsakos, a rich Greek city on the Asian shore of the Hellespont, struck gold staters for about fifty years in the 4th century BC, from the King's Peace of 387 BC, which left the Asian Greeks under Persia, until Alexander crossed into Asia in 334 BC. The back always shows the city's badge, the front half of the winged horse Pegasus. The front changed with almost every issue: Agnes Baldwin's study of 1924, still the standard work, lists some forty issues, most of them heads of gods and heroes (Zeus, Hermes, Athena, maenads, a facing Silenus, Helios) and a few full scenes, such as the infant Herakles strangling the snakes. Together they read like a small gallery of 4th-century Greek sculpture. Each issue is rare, but the series as a whole appears regularly at auction, which makes it one of the more reachable Greek gold coins of the classical period.

augustus-aureus-gaius-and-lucius-caesar-.note: Augustus had no son, so he adopted his grandsons Gaius and Lucius, the sons of his daughter Julia, and raised them as his heirs. Here they stand in togas with the silver shields and spears the knights gave them when they were named 'leaders of the youth', as Augustus records in his Res Gestae; between them are the ladle and the augur's staff of their priesthoods. Struck at Lugdunum (Lyon) from 2 BC, a little in gold and in vast numbers in silver, it is one of the best-known Roman coins. Neither boy reigned: Lucius died at Massilia in AD 2 and Gaius in Lycia in AD 4, and Augustus turned to Tiberius.

croesus-of-lydia-stater-forepart-of-lion.note: Croesus, king of Lydia from about 561 to 546 BC, whose name still means wealth, is credited with the first coins of pure gold and of pure silver. His father's coins were electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver whose value varied from coin to coin; separating the two metals made money people could trust, and Herodotus wrote that the Lydians were the first to strike gold and silver coins. The lion of the Lydian kings faces a bull; the back is still only two punch marks. The first gold weighed about 10.7 g; a lighter stater of about 8.1 g soon followed, worth ten silver pieces. When Cyrus of Persia took Sardis in 546 BC the Persians kept striking the type until the daric replaced it, so some of these coins are Persian, but excavations at Sardis showed the series began under Croesus himself.

ptolemy-ii-and-arsinoe-ii-mnaieion-jugat.note: A gold coin of almost 28 grams, worth a mina, a hundred silver drachms; hence its name, mnaieion. Ptolemy II married his full sister Arsinoe II around 275 BC, and around 272 BC the pair were made gods, the Theoi Adelphoi, the Sibling Gods. They appear side by side under ΑΔΕΛΦΩΝ, 'of the siblings', his shield behind them. The other side shows his parents, Ptolemy I and Berenice I, the founders of the dynasty, under ΘΕΩΝ, 'of the gods'. Two royal couples and two generations on one coin, struck at Alexandria and kept in issue long after both had died.

Its first dies are signed by Kimon and Euainetos, who also signed the city's silver decadrachms. Historians disagree on how long it was struck: Denyse Bérend, who catalogued the American Numismatic Society's Syracusan coins and wrote the standard die study of this gold, tied it to the war of 406–404 BC, while others see it going on into the 390s and later.

known.detail: 18 coins from 6 obverse and 7 reverse dies (Athena / winged thunderbolt, BASILEOS AGATHOKLEOS).

sources.label: KBR SILVER: Syracuse (Agathocles), gold, 100 litrai (Athena / thunderbolt), after Bérend 1998

agathokles-of-syracuse-drachm-or-half-st.note: Agathokles' gold with Athena in a Corinthian helmet and the winged thunderbolt of Zeus. The legend calls him king, a title he took around 304 BC. Closely linked dies point to one short burst of striking, perhaps from the gold Carthage paid him at the peace of 306/5 BC, worth 300 talents of silver according to the Sicilian historian Diodorus. The Oxford historian Christopher de Lisle (2017) calls it an octobol, two-thirds of a stater; dealers often sell it as 100 litrai. An older idea links it to his daughter Lanassa's wedding to Pyrrhus of Epirus, around 297 BC.

note_sources.label: C. de Lisle, The coinage of Agathokles of Syracuse, Numismatic Chronicle 2017

mytilene-lesbos-hekte-sixth-stater-head-.note: Athena in an Attic helmet and two calves' heads face to face, from the years when Mytilene belonged to the Athenian league. It revolted in 428 BC, and the Athenian historian Thucydides tells how Athens first voted to kill every man in the city, then sent a second ship to cancel the order.

One aureus names his legate Marcus Servilius and shows Libertas, the freedom the conspirators said they had restored. Another shows Lucius Junius Brutus, the ancestor who drove out Rome's last king, with the name of Publius Servilius Casca Longus, the conspirator who struck Caesar first. gold-of-the-republic-aureus-laureate-hea.note: In 43 BC Octavian, not yet twenty, marched on Rome and was made consul in August. This aureus puts his own young bearded head on one side (he kept the beard, it is usually thought, in mourning for Caesar until 39 BC) and on the other the laureate head of Julius Caesar, perpetual dictator and chief priest: the heir, and the man he had sworn to avenge. mithradates-vi-of-pontus-stater-stag-gra.note: Mithradates VI Eupator, king of Pontus from 120 to 63 BC, was the most dangerous enemy Rome faced in the east. His portrait is like no king's before him: hair streaming as if in the wind, in the manner of Alexander. On the back a stag grazes beside the star and crescent of his house, inside a wreath of ivy for Dionysus, whose new incarnation he claimed to be. His gold is rare and was struck mostly during his first war with Rome: dated 89/88 BC, the year of the 'Asian Vespers', when he had the Romans and Italians of Asia killed, and at Pergamon, which he made his capital. Defeated by Pompey, he died at Pantikapaion in 63 BC.

agathokles-of-syracuse-electrum-third-or.note: The largest and last of Agathokles' electrum: Apollo, and his sister Artemis with her quiver, named ΣΩΤΕΙΡΑ, the Saviour. Jenkins put it in his last group, with the least gold, which is why it looks so pale. Historians disagree on the date: older catalogues put it after Agathokles made himself king around 304 BC, but the Oxford historian Christopher de Lisle (2017) argues from the great Camarina hoard that all the electrum had ended before peace with Carthage in 306/5 BC.

antiochus-iii-the-great-octadrachm-apoll.note: Antiochus III came to the throne at eighteen in 223 BC and spent his life rebuilding the empire of Seleucus. In his first years mints from Seleucia on the Tigris to Nisibis struck these heavy gold octadrachms, eight drachms of gold, with his young portrait and Apollo, from whom the dynasty claimed descent, seated on the omphalos and testing an arrow. Then came his great march east, in Alexander's footsteps, to Bactria and India, after which he was called Megas, 'the Great'. Rome broke his power at Magnesia in 190 BC.

pyrrhus-in-sicily-stater-nike-walking.note: Struck at Syracuse in 278–276 BC, when Pyrrhus, king of Epirus and a kinsman of Alexander the Great through Alexander's mother Olympias, came to Sicily to drive out the Carthaginians and was hailed king of Sicily. Athena wears a triple-crested Corinthian helmet decorated with a Pegasus, with earring and necklace, and her owl perched behind her. On the back, under ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ ΠΥΡΡΟΥ (of King Pyrrhus), Nike alights on tiptoe, almost dancing, holding out an oak wreath (the oak of Zeus at Dodona, in Pyrrhus' Epirus) and carrying a trophy of captured armour; an ox skull lies at her feet. The pairing recalls Alexander's Athena and Nike staters, but the Syracusan engraver, whose name is not known, gave it a grace Alexander's never had. It is extremely rare. The victories did not last: Pyrrhus left Sicily in 276 BC, saying, according to Plutarch, 'What a wrestling ground we are leaving for Carthage and Rome.' A gold drachm with Artemis and the same Nike was struck beside it.

athens-drachm-or-half-stater-owl-and-twi.note:
The gold version of the Athenian owl. Athens paid its way in silver owls for two centuries and almost never struck gold. From the 430s BC it had dedicated golden Victories (Nikai) on the Acropolis for its sea victories, each carrying about two talents of gold, some 50 kg, in removable sheets over a carved core. In 407/6 BC, losing the Peloponnesian War and short of silver after Sparta took the mines at Laurion, the city melted them down: the historians Hellanikos and Philochoros date the gold coinage to the archon Antigenes, 'from the golden Victories'. Plated bronze followed a year later.

This card covers the whole issue, struck in several sizes with the same Athena and the inscription ΑΘΕ. The stater (about 8.6 g) has a single owl with an olive branch; one sold at NAC in Zurich (auction 77, lot 46) was described as only the fifth known. The drachm (about 4.3 g, the coin shown) has the owl and twig. The tiny diobol (about 1.4 g, 8.5 mm) has two owls facing each other over an olive branch; one sold at Nomos in Zurich in November 2025 for CHF 130,000 before fees, five times its estimate. Paris also has an obol of 0.7 g. All are very rare, and several of the known coins are in museums. The famous silver owl tetradrachm is among the Featured coins.
athens-drachm-or-half-stater-owl-and-twi.examples_note: Athens struck its gold owls in one emergency issue in 407–406 BC, so few survive. The museum coins below cover three sizes: the drachm, the diobol and the obol.
athens-drachm-or-half-stater-owl-and-twi.specimens_note: The two-owls diobol sold in 2025, then the coins in Paris: the drachm (4.30 g), a diobol (1.42 g) and an obol (0.71 g). No open photo of the stater is available yet.

lysimachus-stater-athena.note: Lysimachus, one of Alexander's bodyguards, became governor of Thrace after Alexander's death, then king, and after the battle of Ipsus in 301 BC ruled much of Asia Minor too. Around 297 BC he put Alexander on his coins: the dead king as a god, his hair swept back, with the ram's horn of Zeus Ammon, whose oracle at Siwa had greeted him as the god's son. It is the most famous portrait of Alexander to survive from antiquity. On the back Athena sits holding a small Victory, with 'of King Lysimachus'. Lysimachus fell at Corupedium in 281 BC, but his coin outlived him: Byzantium and the Black Sea cities went on striking it for two centuries.

pantikapaion-stater-facing-satyr.note: Struck at Pantikapaion, capital of the Bosporan Kingdom in the Crimea, under King Leukon I. The bearded head has long been read as Pan, a pun on the city's name, but its features are those of a satyr, probably a nod to Satyros I, the founder of the ruling Spartokid dynasty. The griffin with a spear in its mouth recalls the beasts that Herodotus and Pliny the Elder said guarded the gold of Scythia from the one-eyed Arimaspians. On these staters the satyr is almost always in profile. For one extremely rare issue the engraver turned him three-quarters towards us, following the fashion for facing heads that Kimon's Arethusa at Syracuse had started, and it is the one such coin often ranked beside Kimon's masterpiece. Godfrey Locker Lampson, who owned a coin from the same dies, called the head 'a marvel of speaking portraiture' and said that if he had to pick one coin as the work of the greatest of all die-engravers, it would be this one. The coin in the photo is thought to be the only one of these in private hands. It was in the Hermitage in St Petersburg until the Soviet government sold it among the museum's 'duplicates' in 1934, then belonged to the French collector Charles Gillet, and was bought privately from Bank Leu in 1991. It set the record for an ancient coin twice: $3.25 million (before fees) in the Prospero collection sale in New York in January 2012, and 5.39 million Swiss francs with fees (about $6.0 million) at Numismatica Ars Classica in Zurich in May 2023 (sale 138, lot 155, estimate CHF 1.25 million). Another, better centred, was recovered from smugglers by Greek police in Athens in September 2023 and is kept at the Numismatic Museum there, and the Royal Library of Belgium holds three. The coins name the city, not the king: MacDonald dates this issue c. 370–355 BC, in Leukon I's reign, while NAC and the Royal Library of Belgium give c. 350–300 BC, which could put it under his successors.

brutus-aureus-eid-mar.note: The most famous coin of antiquity, struck by Brutus in 42 BC to celebrate the murder of Julius Caesar on the Ides of March 44 BC: the cap given to freed slaves, between the two daggers. Only three gold examples are known. One is in the collection of the Deutsche Bundesbank in Frankfurt. The second, pierced at the top so it could be worn, was on loan to the British Museum from 2010 to 2021; Numismatica Ars Classica sold it in Zurich on 30 May 2022 for CHF 2.2 million before the buyer's fee, and it is now in a private collection. The third appeared in 2020 and sold for $3.49 million (£2.7 million; about $4.2 million, or £3.24 million, with the buyer's fee), the highest price ever paid for an ancient coin at the time; it then turned out to have a falsified ownership history. The Manhattan District Attorney seized it and returned it to Greece in March 2023, the auction house's owner pleaded guilty in New York, and the firm closed in 2024. The British Museum's own gold example, given by King George IV in 1825, is now known to be a forgery, as the auction house Numismatica Ars Classica noted in 2022. The silver denarius is rare too: about €120,000–€580,000 at auction (middle 80% of 8 sales, 2005–2026, with buyer's fee).

eucratides-i-20-stater-eukratideion.note: The largest gold coin of the ancient world: 169 grams and 58 millimetres across, worth twenty ordinary staters. Eucratides seized the Greek kingdom of Bactria, in today's Afghanistan, around 170 BC, and struck this piece to show off his wealth and his title 'the Great King'. It is the only one known. It came to light in Bukhara in the 1860s, was bought for the collection of Napoleon III, and has been in the Cabinet des médailles in Paris ever since.

maxentius-aureus-facing-bust-ostia.note: Only two coins of this type are known. Roman coins almost never showed the emperor face on in the West until late in Constantine's reign, so a facing portrait from Maxentius, whose coinage otherwise looked to tradition, is a real surprise; Licinius and Constantine later struck facing-head gold of their own. The credit may belong to an engraver rather than the emperor: the scholar Fred Albertson argued that the man who cut these dies had been the chief engraver at Rome before moving to Maxentius's new mint at Ostia, Rome's harbour, opened in 308 or 309 to add to the capital's output from a fortified town close to the sea. The date is debated, from 308 to 312; one reading ties the legend, 'the eternal victory of our emperor', to the recovery of Africa from the rebel Alexander of Carthage around 310. Both known coins, struck from the same pair of dies, come from the Arras (Beaurains) hoard, found in northern France in 1922. The one photographed here (5.51 g) was in the Jameson collection and passed through Ratto (1923), Hess-Leu (1961), Leu (2005) and Numismatica Ars Classica (2011, CHF 625,000), then sold there again in November 2023 for CHF 700,000 before fees (estimate CHF 500,000). The other (5.24 g) belonged to the archaeologist Sir Arthur Evans, the excavator of Knossos, and later to the L. Avot collection, sold through Leu (1979) and Sotheby's (1990 and 1995), and made CHF 600,000 at NAC in May 2024.

brutus-aureus-casca-trophy.note: Brutus's own portrait, struck for his army in the east in 43 or 42 BC, in the months before he and Cassius were beaten at Philippi. The reverse names Publius Servilius Casca Longus, the conspirator who struck Caesar the first blow on the Ides of March and now served as Brutus's officer, signing the gold. Putting his own face on coins sat oddly with the man who killed Caesar for acting like a king, and Cassius never did it. Brutus struck two portrait aurei; NAC judged this sober issue a truer likeness than the idealised one struck for him by Pedanius Costa, perhaps truer even than the EID MAR, showing a man of about forty-three. Very rare. The coin photographed (8.12 g, ex Münzen und Medaillen 1957 and Galerie des Monnaies 1977) sold at NAC in 2013 for CHF 850,000 before fees, for the collection of Sheikh Saoud Al Thani, and again in 2016 for CHF 475,000. Another (8.07 g, ex Biaggi), perhaps the finest known, made CHF 900,000 in 2015.
brutus-aureus-casca-trophy.specimens_note: Two coins of this type have sold for more than $500,000: the 8.12 g coin above (2013) and this 8.07 g coin (2015).

probus-medallion-crossing-the-rhine.note: Apparently unique: the only gold medallion of Probus known. Proclaimed emperor by the eastern army in 276, Probus outlasted his rival Florian, drove the Alamanni and Franks back over the Rhine, put down the usurpers Saturninus, Proculus and Bonosus, and held a triumph in Rome in 281. The next year his own soldiers murdered him at Sirmium. This 26 g gold piece was a gift for officers, probably for that triumph, and is dated by his fourth consulship. On the front Probus, in a consul's robes, shares the portrait with Hercules, a pairing Diocletian and Maximian later made their own. On the back the emperor crosses the Rhine on a pontoon bridge, led by Victory and followed by Mars and his men, with the river god in the waves below. It was the banner image of the Swiss dealer Tkalec's website in the late 1990s, and sold at Numismatica Ars Classica in Zurich in May 2023 for CHF 2.4 million before fees (estimate CHF 800,000), the highest price for Roman gold in our Most expensive coins list.

known.detail: Of the twelve recorded by NAC, seven are in museums and five in private hands.

sources.label: NAC Auction 132 (30 May 2022), lot 481
NAC Auction 83 (20 May 2015), lot 509
NAC Auction 34 (2006), lot 6

ahenobarbus-aureus-temple-of-neptune.note: Ahenobarbus was condemned under the Lex Pedia of 43 BC as one of those behind Caesar's murder, though Suetonius says he was innocent. He joined Brutus and Cassius, commanded a fleet for them, kept it after Philippi and struck gold with the temple of Neptune for his naval victory. It is among the most expensive ancient coins ever sold.

obv.english: Syra(cuse)

syracuse-10-litrai-athena-gorgoneion.note: The smallest of Syracuse's first gold coins: 10 litrai, about two-thirds of a gram and 10 mm across, worth a silver didrachm, with Athena on one side and Medusa's face on her aegis on the other. Berlin's coin cabinet dates it from about 406 BC, as Dionysios I came to power; the American Numismatic Society's catalogue puts it a little earlier, 415–405 BC.

athens-tetradrachm-owl-silver.note: The coin of classical Athens and the best-known ancient coin of all. Paid for by the silver mines at Laurion, owls financed the Parthenon and the fleet and were trusted all round the Mediterranean; in Aristophanes' Birds, owls nest in every purse. They were struck in huge numbers for two centuries, so they are still within reach and turn up in almost every auction. Collectors prize a well-centred strike with the full crest of the helmet and an old, natural toning; many have been over-cleaned. The owl story below follows the coin era by era and shows the copies to know about.
athens-tetradrachm-owl-silver.specimens_note: The finest owls seen at auction in autumn 2026 (dealer photos, linked from the sale), then owls in the Berlin coin cabinet and the Metropolitan Museum.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

melekiathon-of-kition-hemistater-herakle.note: The first gold of Kition. The chunky, muscular Herakles and the lion on the stag's back are Greek in style, but the legend is Phoenician, a mix typical of Cyprus, where Greek and Phoenician kings ruled side by side.

obv.latin: Flavius Iulius Constans Pius Felix Augustus
obv.english: Flavius Julius Constans, dutiful and fortunate Augustus

constans-medallion-of-one-and-a-half-sol.note: Struck at Trier around the winter of 342–343, when Constans crossed the Channel in midwinter to deal with trouble in Britain. The engraver misspelled the legend: EXERCTVS for EXERCITVS, 'the glory of the army'.

obv.latin: Dominus Noster Valentinianus Pius Felix Augustus
obv.english: Our lord Valentinian, dutiful and fortunate Augustus

valentinian-i-medallion-of-four-and-a-ha.note: A 34 mm gold piece of over 19 grams, struck at Antioch. The Berlin coin, the RIC example, was found at Temesvár (Timișoara) in Romania, beyond the Danube frontier: such medallions often went as gifts to barbarian chiefs, who wore them as jewellery.

nectanebo-ii-stater-horse-and-nefer-nub.note: One of the very few coins ever struck with Egyptian hieroglyphs, and the only gold coinage of the native pharaohs. It was made to the weight of the Persian daric, almost certainly to pay the Greek mercenaries who defended the last native pharaohs against Persia. Examples are in Berlin (the coin shown), the British Museum and San Antonio, and very few reach the market.

obv.english: Didia Clara Augusta

didius-julianus-aureus-didia-clara-hilar.note: Didius Julianus famously bought the empire when the Praetorian Guard auctioned it to the highest bidder in March 193, and was killed 66 days later. In that short reign his daughter Didia Clara was made Augusta and given her own coins, among the rarest of all Roman empresses'. The reverse promises 'the cheerfulness of the times'.

obv.latin: Imperator Caesar Marcus Aurelius Quintillus Augustus
obv.english: Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Quintillus Augustus

quintillus-aureus-fides.note: Quintillus, brother of Claudius II, was proclaimed emperor at Milan when Claudius died of plague in 270 and lasted a few weeks, perhaps seventeen days, before the army chose Aurelian instead. His gold is among the rarest of the third century: a handful of aurei from Milan, all with the same bust. 'The loyalty of the army' was the one thing he needed and did not get. No open museum photo is known; the type is recorded from auction sales (NAC 34, 125 and 141).

obv.latin: Imperator Caesar Marcus Aurelius Quintillus Augustus
obv.english: Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Quintillus Augustus

quintillus-aureus-concordia.note: 'The concord of the army': the second of the three reverse designs on Quintillus's Milan aurei, with the officina letter T below. Two coins are recorded in sales (NAC 52 and 135); no open museum photo is known.

obv.english: Cyre(ne)

cyrene-half-stater-rider-and-silphium.note: Cyrene's wealth was silphium, a plant that grew nowhere else, prized as a spice and a medicine and extinct by Nero's day. The city put it on its coins for three centuries. This half stater of the years after Alexander pairs it with a young rider, perhaps one of the horse-breeding aristocrats of the Libyan plateau, and names the magistrate of the year.

obv.english: Chairios (the magistrate)

cyrene-half-stater-ophellas-rider-and-si.note: Struck while Ophellas, Ptolemy's general, governed Cyrene for Egypt (322–313 BC), and signed by the magistrate Chaireos. The little insect beside the silphium is the engraver's touch. The coin shown, from the same dies as the Boston museum's, sold at Nomos in June 2025.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

cyrene-tetrobol-magas-rider-with-star-an.note: Magas, Ptolemy I's stepson, governed Cyrene from 308 BC and made himself its king, holding it against Egypt until his death in 250. His small gold keeps the rider and the silphium of the old city coinage, with a star added in the field.

known.detail: All five come from one obverse die and two reverse dies.

sources.label: KBR SILVER: Gela, gold, double litrae (rider / man-headed bull), after Jenkins 1970, 490-490A
G. K. Jenkins, The Coinage of Gela (AMuGS II, Berlin 1970), nos. 490-490A

gela-dilitron-horseman-and-man-headed-bu.note: Gela's heaviest gold coin, struck in the city's last free months, when Carthage was marching along the south coast of Sicily after destroying Akragas. The rider recalls Gela's famous cavalry; the bull with a man's face is the river Gelas that gave the city its name. Jenkins's die study knows only five coins, all from a single obverse die.

known.detail: All four come from one pair of dies.

sources.label: KBR SILVER: Gela, gold, litrae (forepart of horse / nymph), after Jenkins 1970, 491
G. K. Jenkins, The Coinage of Gela (1970), no. 491

gela-litra-forepart-of-horse-and-sosipol.note: The smallest of Gela's three gold coins, from the same emergency of 406–405 BC. Sosipolis means 'saviour of the city': a goddess the people of Gela turned to as Carthage approached, named on the coin so no one could miss the prayer. Jenkins's die study records four coins.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

obv.english: Gelas (the river god of Gela)

known.detail: 31 coins from one obverse and three reverse dies.

sources.label: KBR SILVER: Gela, gold, third litrae (man-headed bull / Sosipolis), after Jenkins 1970, 492-494
G. K. Jenkins, The Coinage of Gela (1970), nos. 492-494

gela-litra-and-a-third-man-headed-bull-a.note: The commonest of Gela's gold, though 'common' here means about thirty coins known, all from one obverse die. The river-god Gelas on one side and the city's protecting goddess Sosipolis on the other: the whole of Gela's hope in 406–405 BC, before Dionysios of Syracuse failed to save it and its people left the city to Carthage.

known.detail: All three come from one pair of dies; it is the earliest Sicilian gold in the forum's table.

sources.label: KBR SILVER: Messana, gold, dilitrai (biga / springing hare) (455-451 BCE), after Caccamo Caltabiano 1993, no. 321
NAC Auction 138 (18 May 2023), lot 66

messana-dilitron-mule-biga-and-hare.note: One of the earliest gold coins of Sicily, struck about 455–451 BC, half a century before the emergency gold of 406. The mule cart remembers the tyrant Anaxilas, who won the mule-cart race at Olympia; the leaping hare, which he was said to have brought to Sicily, became the city's badge. Only three coins are known.

obv.english: Pelorias (the nymph of Cape Peloron)

known.detail: The single known coin is Caccamo Caltabiano 641 itself; NAC sold it in 1996 and 2006.

sources.label: NAC Auction 33 (5 Apr 2006), lot 79
M. Caccamo Caltabiano, La monetazione di Messana (AMuGS XIII, 1993), no. 641

messana-dilitron-pelorias-and-rearing-ho.note: Pelorias is the nymph of Cape Peloro, the headland at the tip of Sicily facing Italy across the Strait of Messina. Only one coin of this type is known. Caltabiano's die study dates it 411–408 BC; NAC, which sold it, thought it was struck around 400–396 BC, when Carthage was threatening Messana itself.

the-first-coins-electrum-plain-globule.note: The beginning of coinage: lumps of electrum, the natural gold-silver alloy of the Lydian rivers, made to a fixed weight and struck into punches on one side only, with nothing yet on the other. Found with the earliest picture coins in the Artemision at Ephesus, about 650–600 BC. Nothing to look at, which is the point; the most traded early electrum at auction, in every size from the trite (4.7 g) down to tiny 1/96 pieces.

anastasius-solidus.note: Anastasius reformed the bronze coinage and left the treasury full; his solidi continue the late Roman design unchanged.

justin-i-solidus.note: Justin, an illiterate peasant soldier who rose to emperor, introduced the angel that replaced Victory on the solidus.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

justin-justinian-solidus.note: Struck for the few months in 527 when Justin shared the throne with his nephew Justinian.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

justinian-solidus.note: Justinian reconquered Italy and North Africa and built Hagia Sophia. He turned the emperor's portrait to face the viewer, the Byzantine way ever after.

justinian-tremissis.note: A third of a solidus, the small gold of Justinian's age, when his generals won back North Africa and Italy. Struck in large numbers, it is the easiest way into Justinian's gold.

justin-ii-solidus.note: Justin II, Justinian's nephew, lost his mind after Persian victories in 573; his wife Sophia ruled for him.

tiberius-ii-solidus.note: Tiberius II put the cross on steps on the solidus, the reverse that dominated Byzantine gold for a century; it recalls the cross set up on Golgotha.

maurice-solidus.note: Maurice reformed the army and ended the Persian war, but was overthrown by mutinous troops and executed with his sons.

phocas-solidus.note: Phocas, the centurion who overthrew Maurice, brought the beard back to the emperor's portrait. His rule ended with his execution by Heraclius.

heraclius-solidus.note: Heraclius saved the empire from Persia and brought back the True Cross to Jerusalem in 630, only to lose Syria and Egypt to the Arabs.

heraclius-three-solidus.note: The three-figure solidi show Heraclius with long beard and moustache between his two sons.

constans-ii-solidus.note: Constans II moved the court to Syracuse in Sicily and was murdered in his bath there in 668.

constantine-iv-solidus.note: Constantine IV held off the great Arab siege of Constantinople (674–678), helped by Greek fire.

justinian-ii-christ-solidus.note: In 692 Justinian II put Christ on a coin for the first time, and moved himself to the back, calling himself 'servant of Christ'. The caliph Abd al-Malik answered with the first all-text Islamic dinars.

justinian-ii-second-solidus.note: Deposed and with his nose cut off in 695, Justinian II returned in 705 with an army of Bulgars. His second-reign coins show a different, curly-haired Christ.

leontius-solidus.note: Leontius overthrew Justinian II and was overthrown in turn by Tiberius III.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

tiberius-iii-solidus.note: Tiberius III was an admiral who seized the throne in 698 after a failed expedition to save Carthage from the Arabs. Justinian II, whose nose had been cut off when he was deposed, came back with a Bulgar army in 705 and later had him executed. The cross on steps recalls the one on Golgotha.

philippicus-solidus.note: Philippicus, an Armenian general, overthrew Justinian II in 711 and spent two years reviving a religious quarrel before army officers blinded him in 713.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

leo-iii-solidus.note: Leo III beat the second Arab siege of Constantinople (717–718) and began Iconoclasm, the ban on religious images. Christ disappears from the coins.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

constantine-v-solidus.note: Three generations on one coin: Constantine V, his son, and his dead father on the back.

irene-solidus.note: Irene blinded her own son to rule alone, the first woman to reign over the empire in her own name. Her solidus shows her on both sides; the Pope's coronation of Charlemagne in 800 was partly justified by the claim that the throne was empty.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

nikephoros-i-solidus.note: Nikephoros I was killed in battle by the Bulgar khan Krum, who made a drinking cup of his skull.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

michael-ii-solidus.note: Michael II was in prison awaiting execution when his friends murdered Leo V in church on Christmas Day 820 and crowned him, still in his chains. His son Theophilos is on the back.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

theophilos-solidus.note: Theophilos, the last iconoclast emperor, loved splendour: golden mechanical lions roared beside his throne.

michael-iii-solidus.note: With the end of Iconoclasm in 843, Christ returned to the gold coinage.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

basil-i-solidus.note: Basil, a peasant groom from Macedonia, murdered his patron Michael III to found the Macedonian dynasty, the empire's most glorious.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

leo-vi-solidus.note: Leo VI, a scholar emperor, rewrote the laws of the empire.

alexander-solidus.note: Alexander reigned for a year; his solidus shows his patron saint crowning him.

constantine-vii-zoe-solidus.note: Struck while Zoe Karbonopsina ruled for her small son: the boy emperor and his mother share the cross, the empress in the jewelled loros.

romanos-i-solidus-crowned-by-christ.note: Romanos, the admiral who made himself emperor, shows Christ crowning him; on the back his own son Christopher takes the place of honour over the rightful heir, Constantine VII.

constantine-vii-romanus-solidus.note: Romanos I Lekapenos, an admiral, pushed the young Constantine VII aside for twenty years.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

constantine-vii-solidus.note: Constantine VII 'Born in the Purple' wrote the Book of Ceremonies and On the Administration of the Empire.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

nikephoros-ii-histamenon.note: Nikephoros II, the 'White Death of the Saracens', reconquered Crete and Antioch, and split the gold coin into the full-weight histamenon and the lighter tetarteron.

john-i-histamenon.note: John Tzimiskes murdered his uncle Nikephoros II and then beat the Rus' prince Sviatoslav on the Danube.

basil-ii-histamenon.note: Basil II 'the Bulgar-Slayer' reigned for almost fifty years and left the empire at its medieval peak. His gold, struck in enormous numbers, is among the most common Byzantine coins.

romanos-iii-histamenon.note: Romanos III put the Virgin on the front of the coin; he was later found drowned in his bath.

michael-iv-histamenon.note: Michael IV, a peasant's son from Paphlagonia, became emperor in 1034 by marrying the empress Zoe the day her husband Romanos III died. The hand of God reaches down to crown him. He suffered from epilepsy and died a monk in 1041.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

constantine-ix-histamenon.note: Constantine IX reigned during the Great Schism of 1054 between Rome and Constantinople. His histamena are the first to be slightly cup-shaped.

theodora-histamenon.note: Theodora, last of the Macedonian dynasty, ruled alone in her seventies.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

isaac-i-histamenon.note: Isaac I, a general, was criticised for showing himself with a sword, as if he owed his throne to force rather than to God.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

constantine-x-histamenon.note: Under Constantine X the gold coinage began to be debased, a sign of the troubles ahead.

romanos-iv-histamenon.note: Romanos IV was defeated and captured by the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan at Manzikert in 1071, opening Anatolia to the Turks.

michael-vii-histamenon.note: Michael VII's gold fell to about two-thirds pure; people nicknamed him 'Parapinakes', minus a quarter, for the price of wheat.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

alexios-i-hyperpyron.note: Alexios I restored the empire and in 1092 replaced the debased coinage with the new cup-shaped hyperpyron, 'highly refined' gold. He called on the West for help, and got the First Crusade.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

john-ii-hyperpyron.note: John II 'the Good', admired even by his enemies, spent his reign campaigning.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

manuel-i-hyperpyron.note: Manuel I loved the West, jousted in tournaments, and lost the battle of Myriokephalon to the Seljuks in 1176. His coins show the young beardless Christ Emmanuel, a play on his own name.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

andronikos-i-hyperpyron.note: Andronikos I, a charming adventurer, seized the throne at 65 and was torn apart by the Constantinople mob two years later.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

isaac-ii-hyperpyron.note: Isaac II was blinded and deposed by his brother; his son's appeal to the crusaders led to the sack of 1204.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

alexios-iii-hyperpyron.note: Alexios III fled as the Fourth Crusade reached Constantinople in 1203. The city fell the next year, and this catalogue stops there.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

anastasius-ii-solidus.note: Anastasius II, a civil servant made emperor by the army, prepared Constantinople for the great Arab siege and was deposed after two years.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

theodosius-iii-solidus.note: Theodosius III, a tax collector forced onto the throne by mutinous troops, stepped down for Leo III and became a bishop.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

leo-iv-solidus.note: Four emperors of one family on a single coin: the living father and son on the front, the dead grandfather and great-grandfather on the back.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

constantine-vi-irene-solidus.note: Irene ruled for her son Constantine VI; in 797 she had him blinded and took the throne herself.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

staurakios-solidus.note: Staurakios was crowned in 803; his father was killed by the Bulgars in 811 and Staurakios himself, badly wounded, lasted only a few months.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

michael-i-solidus.note: Michael I recognised Charlemagne as emperor of the west in 812, then lost to the Bulgars and retired to a monastery.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

leo-v-solidus.note: Leo V, a general, revived Iconoclasm and was murdered in the palace chapel on Christmas Day 820.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

romanos-ii-solidus.note: Romanos II, son of Constantine VII, married the innkeeper's daughter Theophano; his reign saw Crete won back from the Arabs. No solidus in his own name alone is known: his gold of 959 re-used his father's dies, with the legend re-cut (Füeg).

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

constantine-viii-histamenon.note: Constantine VIII, Basil II's younger brother, reigned alone for three years after fifty as junior co-emperor.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

zoe-theodora-histamenon.note: In April 1042 the people of Constantinople rose against Michael V and put the two elderly sisters of the Macedonian house on the throne together. Their joint coins, struck for a few weeks, are very rare.

michael-vi-histamenon.note: Michael VI, an elderly official chosen by Theodora on her deathbed, was overthrown by the generals within a year.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

eudokia-histamenon.note: Widowed in 1067, the empress Eudokia ruled for her sons for a few months, then married the general Romanos Diogenes.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

nikephoros-iii-histamenon.note: Nikephoros III struck gold barely half pure, a sign of the crisis that Alexios I would end with the hyperpyron.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

justinian-solidus-rome.note: Struck in Rome within a few years of its recapture from the Goths; the R under the reverse marks the mint. Extremely rare.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

justinian-solidus-ravenna.note: Ravenna's gold under Justinian, struck in the city where his mosaic portrait with Theodora still shines in San Vitale.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

constantine-iv-solidus-ravenna.note: The Ravenna version of Constantine IV's solidus, dated by the tax year (671/2 on the coin shown).

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

justinian-solidus-carthage.note: One of the first gold coins of reconquered Africa, struck at Carthage six years after Belisarius took the city from the Vandals and dated to the tax year 539/540.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

constans-ii-solidus-carthage.note: A typical Carthage solidus of the last decades: only 15 mm across but full weight, so it is unusually thick. Extremely rare.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

constans-ii-solidus-syracuse.note: Struck at Syracuse around 668, the year Constans II, who had made the city his capital, was murdered in his bath there.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

philippicus-solidus-syracuse.note: Philippicus, an Armenian general who overthrew Justinian II, reigned two years before he was blinded. His gold from Syracuse is far rarer than that of Constantinople.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

theophilus-solidus-syracuse.note: A Sicilian solidus with the emperor on both sides, struck while the Arab conquest of Sicily, begun in 827, crept towards Syracuse.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

justinian-solidus-thessalonica.note: Thessalonica's version of Justinian's standard solidus, told from the capital's by its style.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

phocas-solidus-thessalonica.note: Phocas's solidus from Thessalonica, a rare provincial version of the capital's design.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

heraclii-revolt-solidus.note: Struck for the rebellion against Phocas: father and son appear as consuls, not emperors, because they did not yet claim the throne. In 610 the son sailed to Constantinople, killed Phocas and became emperor. The mint is debated (Alexandria or Cyprus).

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

justin-ii-solidus-alexandria.note: The Alexandria solidus of Justin II, marked by an I at the end of the reverse legend.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

variant_list.ref: Dionysius I of Syracuse Syracuse SNG ANS 361-375

obv.english: Of the Syracusans

syracuse-decadrachm-euainetos.note: These large ten-drachm pieces are thought to celebrate Syracuse's victory over the Athenian invasion of 415–413 BC. Euainetos' Arethusa, her hair full of dolphins and reeds, was copied across the Greek world.

variant_list.ref: Dionysius I of Syracuse Syracuse SNG ANS 357-360

obv.english: Of the Syracusans

syracuse-decadrachm-kimon.note: Kimon signed his name in tiny letters on Arethusa's headband, one of the first artist's signatures in Western art.

obv.english: Of the Syracusans

syracuse-demareteion.note: Named after Queen Damarete, who according to the Greek historian Diodorus was given a gold crown by the Carthaginians after the battle of Himera (480 BC) in return for her help with the peace. One of the most famous coins of the ancient world, and very rare.

variant_list.ref: Dionysius I of Syracuse Syracuse Fischer-Bossert II. 78-81

obv.english: Arethusa (the nymph)

syracuse-tetradrachm-kimon-facing.note: Kimon's facing Arethusa is often called the most beautiful Greek coin; the facing head was a daring choice, since the nose was the first thing to wear down.

syracuse-tetradrachm-eukleidas-athena.note: Eukleidas' Athena, in a helmet with three crests, was the model for Kimon's facing Arethusa.

syracuse-tetradrachm-euainetos.note: The classic Syracusan tetradrachm of the late 5th century BC, from dies signed by Euainetos.

specimens.t: The MacDonald 31 plate coin · Künker 383/2025 · 9.09 g · hammer €95,000

pantikapaion-stater-first-satyr-griffin.note: The first gold coins of Pantikapaion, struck early in the reign of Leukon I, when the grain trade with Athens was making the Bosporan kings rich. The satyr is in profile with wild, unwreathed hair; on the other side the griffin that guarded the gold of Scythia stands on an ear of corn. A few years later one rare issue turned the satyr to face us (its own card); from about 355 BC the satyr wears an ivy wreath (its own card).
pantikapaion-stater-first-satyr-griffin.specimens_note: The Berlin coin, and the coin MacDonald illustrates for this type (sold by Künker in 2023).

cyrene-stater-quadriga-and-zeus-ammon.note: Cyrene, the Greek city in Libya, grew rich on silphium, a plant so prized as medicine and seasoning that it was eaten to extinction. In the late 4th century BC, in the troubled years after Alexander, it struck its own gold: a racing chariot, the pride of Cyrene's horse-breeders, whose teams won at Olympia and Delphi, and Zeus Ammon, the ram-horned god of the Libyan desert oracle that Alexander had visited.

obv.english: Constantine the greatest Augustus

constantine-i-medallion-of-six-solidi.note: Apparently unique and unrecorded: a 27 g gold piece worth six solidi, struck at Nicomedia for Constantine's tricennalia, the thirtieth year of his reign, in 335. The only parallels known come from the mint of Trier. Gold multiples like this were handed out to the army at the New Year and at great celebrations, the surest way to keep the soldiers loyal. Constantine had much to celebrate: he had beaten every rival, built a new capital at Constantinople and made Christianity the favoured religion, and in 335 he made his nephew Delmatius a Caesar and his nephew Hannibalianus a king, to secure the dynasty. Two years later he was dead. His sons purged the family, killing Delmatius and Hannibalianus; Constantine II died fighting his brother Constans in 340, and Constans was murdered in 350. Ex Gorny & Mosch 215 (2013), lot 1095; sold at Numismatica Ars Classica in Zurich in November 2022 for CHF 800,000 before fees (estimate CHF 350,000).

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

known.detail: 41 coins from 6 obverse and 24 reverse dies (Jenkins & Lewis series IX).

sources.label: KBR SILVER: Carthage, gold, tridrachms (265-255 BCE), Jenkins & Lewis 1963 series IX
G. K. Jenkins and R. B. Lewis, Carthaginian Gold and Electrum Coins (RNS, London 1963)

carthage-trihemistater-tanit-horse-looki.note: The largest regular Carthaginian gold coin, worth a stater and a half, struck in the years just before the First Punic War broke out in 264 BC. The horse turning to look back is one of the most graceful animals on any ancient coin.

carthage-tenth-stater-palm-tree-horse-he.note: One of Carthage's first gold coins, under a gram and 9 mm across, yet carrying the city's two emblems: the palm tree (phoinix, the Greek word for both the tree and the Phoenicians) and the horse's head of the founding legend.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

known.detail: 91 coins from 43 obverse and 57 reverse dies (Jenkins & Lewis series V).

sources.label: KBR SILVER: Carthage, electrum, staters (310-290 BCE), Jenkins & Lewis 1963 series V

carthage-electrum-stater-tanit-standing-.note: Struck in pale gold mixed with silver, around the time Agathocles of Syracuse landed in Africa and marched on Carthage (310 BC). Huge numbers were made to pay soldiers, so this is the Carthaginian gold most often seen today.

carthage-electrum-half-stater-horse-befo.note: The half stater puts all of Carthage's emblems together: Tanit, the horse and the palm tree.

obv.english: Leukippos (the magistrate)

known.detail: Five coins from 3 obverse and 4 reverse dies (Pyrrhic-war gold, 280s BC).

sources.label: KBR SILVER: Metapontum, gold, third staters (285-275 BCE), after Johnston 1990

metapontum-third-stater-leukippos-barley.note: Metapontum, a Greek city on the instep of Italy, grew rich on grain, and an ear of barley was its badge for three centuries. It struck gold only in emergencies. This third stater belongs to the war of 280–279 BC, when Pyrrhus of Epirus came over to fight Rome for the Greek cities of the south. The helmeted hero is Leukippos, honoured as the city's founder.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

obv.english: Constantine the greatest Augustus

constantine-i-medallion-of-two-solidi.note: A double solidus for Constantine's twentieth year as emperor, celebrated first at the Council of Nicaea in 325 and again in Rome in 326. Medallions like this were not money for the market but gifts, handed out by the emperor to officers and officials on great occasions.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

obv.english: Our lord Valens the greatest Augustus

rev.latin: Dominus Noster Valens Victor Semper Augustus
rev.english: Our lord Valens the victor, ever Augustus

known.detail: Künker called its 62 g medallion in an ancient mount 'Wohl Unikum' (probably unique); a related type is cited only as 'cf. Gnecchi pl. 15, 1'.

sources.label: Künker Auktion 158 (28 Sep 2009), lot 839

valens-medallion-of-nine-solidi.note: Probably unique: a nine-solidus medallion showing Valens in triumph, still in the ornate gold frame in which an ancient owner wore it. Three years later Valens was killed by the Goths at Adrianople. The weight given includes the mount.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

obv.latin: Imperator Caesar Marcus Aurelius Quintillus Augustus
obv.english: Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Quintillus Augustus

quintillus-aureus-mars.note: Mars the peace-bringer, with an olive branch instead of a trophy: a reverse not in RIC and known from a single coin (NAC 51, 2009), the rarest of Quintillus's three gold designs. No open museum photo is known.

olbia-hemidrachm-demeter-and-dolphin.note: Olbia's only gold, struck around 315–310 BC: the grain goddess of the Black Sea wheat trade on one side and the dolphin that the city's earliest bronze money was cast in the shape of on the other. Karyshkovskij recorded fifteen coins; six were stolen from a museum and melted, and most of the rest are in museums, so about a dozen survive and a handful have been sold (Triton XVI and XIX, NAC 158, Gorny & Mosch 240).

pescennius-niger-aureus-jupiter-seated.note: Jupiter Best and Greatest, Father of the Fatherland: Niger's claim to Rome, struck at Alexandria while Egypt was his. Possibly unique; sold at NAC 52 in 2009. The 'Justus' in his titles is the nickname his soldiers gave him.

obv.latin: Imperator Caesar Gaius Pescennius Niger Iustitia Augusti
obv.english: Emperor Caesar Gaius Pescennius Niger, Justice of the emperor

rev.english: To eternal Rome, father of his country

pescennius-niger-aureus-roma-aeterna.note: Eternal Rome, promised by a man who never reached it. Niger's aurei were struck at Antioch in small numbers for his officers; almost every surviving coin is from different dies. This one sold at Künker 419 in 2025.

corinth-electrum-stater-plain-surface.note: Among the very first coins: a lump of electrum of fixed weight, over 17 grams, with no picture at all, only the marks of the punches that struck it. Struck on Samos in the early 6th century BC; extremely rare.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

obv.english: Our lord Leo eternal Augustus

leo-i-solidus-salus-reipublicae-emperor-.note: One of the great puzzles of late Roman coinage, with only a handful known. Scholars disagree over who stands on the reverse and what the final C means. Grierson and Mays read it as Caesar and date the coin to 470–471, when Leo was forced to make Patricius, son of his overmighty general Aspar, his Caesar; it would then be the only coin of Patricius, who was wounded and deposed when Aspar was murdered in 471. Kent, in RIC, gives it instead to Leo's grandson Leo II in 474.

capua-electrum-three-eighths-shekel-janu.note: After Hannibal's victory at Cannae in 216 BC, much of southern Italy went over to him. His army paid its way in pale gold on the Carthaginian shekel standard, with a design borrowed from Rome's own silver. The coin was long given to Capua, the second city of Italy, which joined Hannibal and was retaken by Rome in 211 BC. Find-spots studied by the Roman coin historian Michael Crawford (2002), and Historia Numorum Italy (2001), the standard catalogue of the region's coins, place it instead with the Carthaginians in Bruttium, the toe of Italy, where Hannibal held out longest.

note_sources.label: CNG, Triton VIII lot 53 (2005): the move from Capua to Bruttium

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

obv.english: Of the people of Cyrene

cyrene-stater-ophellas-quadriga-and-zeus.note: Struck while Ophellas, one of Alexander's officers, governed Cyrene for Ptolemy I after taking the city in 322 BC. Each stater carries the name of the yearly magistrate (here Chaireos). Ophellas later broke with Ptolemy and ruled on his own, until he marched west to join Agathocles of Syracuse against Carthage in 308 BC and was murdered by his ally.

cyrene-drachm-facing-zeus-ammon-silphium.note: A tiny gold coin, only 7 mm across, with one of the boldest facing heads of the Greek world: Zeus Ammon, the ram-horned god of the Libyan desert oracle. On the back is silphium, the wild plant that made Cyrene rich. It was sold all over the Mediterranean as a medicine and seasoning, worth its weight in silver, and was gathered to extinction by Roman times; Pliny says the last stalk was sent to Nero.

cyrene-dilitron-silphium-and-zeus-ammon.note: One of Cyrene's earliest gold coins, from the classical city, about 9 mm across and under 2 g. It pairs the two emblems of Cyrene: silphium, the plant its wealth was built on, and Zeus Ammon, whose oracle at Siwa lay in the desert to the east.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

obv.latin: Imperator Caesar Marcus Didius Iulianus Augustus
obv.english: Emperor Caesar Marcus Didius Julianus Augustus

didius-julianus-aureus-rector-orbis.note: Didius Julianus bought the empire in AD 193, when the Praetorian Guard auctioned the throne after murdering Pertinax. His coins call him RECTOR ORBIS, ruler of the world; he ruled for 66 days before the Senate condemned him and a soldier killed him in the palace. The Vienna coin was pierced to be worn.

akragas-agrigento-gold-eagle-on-hare-cra.note: The eagle seizing a hare is Akragas's most dramatic design, best known from the city's great silver decadrachm and tetradrachms. In the city's last months, as Carthage besieged it in 406 BC, it was struck in gold too, a little heavier than the eagle-and-serpent gold. The coin in the photo is in the Paris coin cabinet.

obv.english: Of the Syracusans

syracuse-dilitron-athena-signed-by-im-an.note: Struck in the winter of 406/5 BC, after Carthage had destroyed Akragas and was marching on Gela, among Syracuse's first gold coins. Its engraver signed his initials, IM, under Athena's neck; on the back Medusa sticks out her tongue from the middle of Athena's snake-fringed aegis. Only seven are known, all from one obverse die.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

syracuse-gold-arethusa-and-octopus.note: A gold coin a third of a gram in weight and 7 mm across, worth one silver drachm: Arethusa on one side and, on the other, the octopus of Syracuse's small silver litrai. The German numismatist Christof Boehringer, who studied the first gold of Sicily, dated the Berlin coin to 408–406 BC, among the city's earliest gold. No other example has turned up.

bosporan-stater-anonymous-augustus-and-a.note: Struck in the years of Queen Dynamis and her successor Aspurgus, when the Bosporan kingdom, Rome's client on the Crimean side of the Black Sea, put the heads of Augustus and his son-in-law Agrippa on its gold instead of its own ruler's. The kingdom's staters were dated by its own era (from 297 BC), so each year's issue can be told apart. Paris's anonymous stater is shown; its exact year was not checked.

bosporan-stater-aspurgus-augustus-and-ag.note: Aspurgus, son of Queen Dynamis's second husband, ruled from AD 15 to 38 under Rome's protection and kept the Augustus and Agrippa types of the anonymous staters, now with his own monogram. Later kings put themselves on the front. No open museum photo was found.

bosporan-stater-mithridates-iii-emperor-.note: Mithridates III (AD 40–43), great-grandson of Mithridates VI of Pontus, fell out with Claudius and was deposed in favour of his brother Kotys. His rare gold shows a Roman-style laureate head and Nike with wreath and palm. No open museum photo was found.

bosporan-stater-kotys-i-agrippina-and-ne.note: Kotys I (AD 46–61) was put on the throne by Claudius after his brother's revolt. His gold carries Agrippina the Younger on one side and her son Nero on the other, with the king reduced to a monogram: the clearest statement on any coin of who really ruled the Bosporus.

bosporan-stater-rhescuporis-i-vespasian-.note: Rhescuporis I (AD 68–93) reigned through the Year of the Four Emperors and the Flavian dynasty; this issue pairs Vespasian with his son Titus. The Bosporan staters were still nearly pure gold, close to the 7.9 g of the Roman aureus.

bosporan-stater-sauromates-i-and-hadrian.note: From Sauromates I (AD 93–124) the kings put their own diademed bust on the front and the reigning emperor, here Hadrian, on the back: the pattern every later Bosporan stater follows.

bosporan-stater-kotys-ii-and-hadrian.note: Kotys II (AD 123–133) with Hadrian, who confirmed him as king. The kingdom's gold still came from its own trade in grain, fish and slaves across the Black Sea.

bosporan-stater-rhoemetalces-and-antonin.note: Rhoemetalces (AD 131–154), a king who visited Rome and was received by Antoninus Pius, whose head takes the back of the stater. Symbols such as a trident or a spearhead mark the year's issue.

bosporan-stater-eupator-marcus-aurelius-.note: Eupator (AD 154–174) ruled when Rome had two emperors, and the back of his stater shows both: Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus facing each other. During his reign the gold began to be alloyed with silver, so museums call his later coins electrum.

bosporan-stater-sauromates-ii-and-septim.note: Sauromates II (AD 174–210) fought the Scythians and Siraces and kept his kingdom's long alliance with Rome; his staters carry Septimius Severus. The metal is now plainly electrum, pale gold mixed with silver.

bosporan-stater-rhescuporis-ii-and-elaga.note: Rhescuporis II (AD 211–227) issued staters with Caracalla, Elagabalus and Severus Alexander in turn; this one shows Elagabalus. Older books number him Rhescuporis III, which is how Paris labels its coins.

bosporan-stater-kotys-iii-and-severus-al.note: Kotys III (AD 227–234) with Severus Alexander. The stater is still electrum here; within a few years the alloy slid to billon and then bronze, and the gold coinage of the Bosporus, begun under Alexander the Great's contemporaries, came to an end.

bosporan-stater-sauromates-iii-and-sever.note: Sauromates III ruled for one year, AD 229–232 by some counts, and his electrum staters with Severus Alexander are the last of the Bosporan gold in this catalogue; the kings after him struck in billon.

pantikapaion-silver-tetradrachm-apollo-a.note: Pantikapaion's largest silver, struck in the same years as its famous gold staters with the satyr and griffin: Apollo, the city's god, and a horse quietly grazing, an image of the Scythian grasslands whose grain made the Bosporus rich. Very rare: the coin shown sold at Nomos in June 2024.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

pantikapaion-silver-drachm-satyr-and-ox-.note: The satyr of the gold staters, here facing the viewer on a silver drachm, with an ox's head on the back. The same facing head appears on hemidrachms with the forepart of a bull (NAC 88, 2015).

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

pantikapaion-silver-diobol-silenos-and-r.note: A small silver piece of the early fourth century: the bald, bearded Silenos who became the city's badge, and the ram's head of the older fractions.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

pantikapaion-silver-diobol-lion-scalp-an.note: The commonest of Pantikapaion's classical silver: a lion's scalp, flattened as if pinned to the wall, and a ram's head. Struck in diobols, hektai and tiny hemiobols from about 430 to 380 BC, with the city's name growing from ΠΑ to ΠΑΝΤΙ.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

pantikapaion-silver-diobol-facing-lion-a.note: Pantikapaion's first coins, from about 480 BC: a lion's head seen from the front and a punch-mark on the back, like the archaic coins of Ionia from which the city's Milesian founders came. Struck as didrachms, trites, diobols and smaller.

_photo.licence: Auction photo, linked from the source

pantikapaion-silver-tetartemorion-ant.note: A quarter-obol of six millimetres with an ant on it, one of the smallest and oddest coins of the Black Sea. Why an ant is not known; it is one of the few insects on any Greek coin.

known.detail: Emergency gold stater of 407-404 BC; NAC called its coin the fifth known.

sources.label: NAC Auction 77 (26 May 2014), lot 46 (8.61 g)

athens-stater-athena-and-owl.note: In 407/6 BC, near the end of the Peloponnesian War, Athens melted the golden statues of Victory on the Acropolis to pay its fleet. The gold went into staters, drachms, hektai and smaller pieces with the owl of the silver coinage. This is the largest, two drachms of gold (8.6 g); the drachm has its own card and the owl guide tells the story. Both Paris coins are from the Luynes and Delepierre collections.

known.detail: Gold diobol (sixth stater) of 407/6 BC with two owls; one is in Berlin.

sources.label: Nomos 37 (16 Nov 2025), lot 107

athens-hekte-two-owls.note: The small change of the emergency gold of 407/6 BC: a sixth of a stater with two owls instead of one, as on the silver diobol. Rarer than the stater and the drachm.

specimens.t: The variety with Zeus Ammon facing

cyrene-gold-obol-zeus-ammon-and-nymph.note: The small change of Cyrene's gold, under a gram, from the years of Alexander's successors: the city's ram-horned Zeus Ammon on one side and a nymph on the other, Kyrene herself if the usual reading is right. The Paris cabinet holds a tray of them, with heads young and old and one with Ammon facing; the three shown are the best struck.

persian-daric-king-running-with-spear-an.note: The gold coin of the Persian empire, struck at Sardis from Darius I to the fall of the empire and known to the Greeks as the 'archer'. Darics paid Greek mercenaries, bribed Greek politicians (Sparta's Agesilaus said he was driven out of Asia by thirty thousand archers) and were melted by Alexander into his own gold. A bridge card (owner's decision, 5 Nov 2026): Persia itself is outside the catalogue, but the daric is Croesus' Sardis mint carried on under new masters, the gold of the Greek East until Alexander, so this one card stands for all of them, as the Seleucid darics stand for Babylon's.

euthydemos-i-octadrachm-herakles-seated.note: Euthydemos, a Greek from Magnesia, seized Bactria around 230 BC and held it through a two-year siege by Antiochus III, who finally recognised him as king. His gold octadrachm, eight drachms of gold, is one of the largest Greek gold coins and among the finest Hellenistic portraits: a heavy, middle-aged face with no flattery in it. Very rare; the stater of the same design has its own card.

pharzoios-olbia-stater-eagle-on-tamga.note: In the first century AD Olbia paid tribute to the Sarmatian kings of the steppe, and for a year or two struck gold in the name of one of them, Pharzoios, with his portrait and his clan's tamga under the Greek eagle. Crude, rare and a document of a Greek city under nomad rule.

orontes-lampsakos-stater-satrap-and-pega.note: Lampsakos struck gold staters with Pegasus for a century; this issue puts a Persian satrap's portrait on the front, one of the earliest portraits of a living man on a coin. The BnF and the older books name him Orontes, the satrap who rebelled against Artaxerxes II; Troxell argued for his kinsman Artabazos, the real satrap of the province, which is why the card says 'a satrap'.

andriskos-stater-herakles.note: Andriskos, a fuller's son from Adramyttion, claimed to be the son of the last king Perseus, raised Macedon against Rome in 149 BC and beat a Roman army before Metellus crushed him the next year. His gold, in the name of 'King Philip', is almost all that survives of the pretender's year. Of the greatest rarity.

thebes-gold-obol-infant-herakles-strangl.note: Thebes, Herakles' birthplace, put the baby hero and Hera's snakes on its silver; this tiny gold obol is the only Theban gold, struck in the city's years of power under Epaminondas. The Paris coin is worn and was once pierced to be worn as a charm.

stymphalos-gold-obol.note: Stymphalos in Arcadia is the lake of Herakles' sixth labour, the man-eating birds. The little city struck a short, fine silver coinage around 350 BC with Artemis and a bird's head, and this gold obol beside it, known from a coin or two.

cyrene-tetradrachm-silphium-and-heart-sh.note: Cyrene's wealth was silphium, a plant that grew only on the Libyan plateau, prized as a spice and a medicine and extinct by Nero's day. The city put it on its silver for three centuries. This is the earliest kind, from the years around 480 BC: the plant on one side and, on the other, its fruit, shaped like a heart, between two dolphins. The heart shape of the fruit is the likeliest origin of the heart symbol.

specimens.t: The earlier, heavier issue of c. 480–460 BC · Berlin 18216670 · 16.57 g

cyrene-tetradrachm-silphium-and-zeus-amm.note: Cyrene's wealth was silphium, a plant that grew only on the Libyan plateau, prized as a spice and a medicine and extinct by Nero's day. The city put it on its silver for three centuries. The classic pairing of the fifth century: the whole plant, leaves, stalk and flower heads drawn like a botanical plate, and Zeus Ammon, the Libyan oracle god the Greeks of Cyrene adopted, with the ram's horn that marks him out.

barke-tetradrachm-silphium-and-facing-ze.note: Barke (Barca), Cyrene's neighbour and rival inland, shared the silphium trade and the coin designs. Its boldest coin turns Zeus Ammon to face the viewer, hair and horns spreading like a mane, a rare facing head that answers the facing Arethusa of Syracuse in the same years.

cyrene-didrachm-magas-apollo-karneios-an.note: The last silphium silver, under Magas, Ptolemy I's stepson, who governed Cyrene for the Ptolemies and then ruled it as king for thirty years. Apollo Karneios, the ram-horned Apollo of the Dorian settlers, replaces Zeus Ammon; the plant on the back is the same as ever.

obv.english: Our lord Anastasius, eternal Augustus

anastasius-tremissis.note: A third of a solidus, the small gold of the first Byzantine emperor. Anastasius reformed the bronze, ended the hated tax on trades and left 320,000 pounds of gold in the treasury. His tremisses keep the late Roman Victory and are among the commonest Byzantine gold coins, a fine first piece of Byzantine gold.

obv.english: Our lord Justin, eternal Augustus

justin-i-tremissis.note: Justin, a Balkan peasant who walked to Constantinople and rose through the palace guard to the throne, kept Anastasius' Victory on his small gold while the solidus took the new angel. His nephew Justinian ran the empire for him.

obv.english: Our lord Tiberius, eternal Augustus

maurice-tremissis.note: Under Maurice the plain cross potent replaced Victory on the tremissis for good: the 'victory of Maurice' in the legend now stands round a Christian cross. Maurice held the Danube and ended the Persian war, then was overthrown and killed with his sons by the mutinous army under Phocas.

specimens.t: Early issue, bearded bust (DOC 17b) · ANS · 1.41 g

obv.english: Our lord Phocas eternal Augustus

phocas-tremissis.note: Phocas, the centurion who murdered Maurice and took the throne, is remembered as the worst of the early Byzantine tyrants; his column still stands in the Roman Forum. His tremisses repeat Maurice's cross, with a bearded bust on the earliest.

obv.english: Our lord Heraclius, eternal Augustus

heraclius-tremissis.note: Heraclius' solidi crowd him with his sons; his tremisses keep a single young bust in profile, the old Roman way, for his whole long reign, through the war that won back the True Cross from Persia and the Arab conquests that followed.

obv.english: Our lord Constantine, eternal Augustus

constans-ii-semissis.note: Half a solidus. Constans II, grandson of Heraclius, lost Egypt and much of the sea to the Arabs, moved his court to Syracuse and was murdered in his bath there in 668. The semissis has the cross on a globe, between the solidus' cross on steps and the tremissis' plain cross.

constantine-ix-tetarteron.note: From Nikephoros II the gold coin came in two kinds, the broad histamenon and the small, thick, slightly lighter tetarteron. Constantine IX, third husband of the empress Zoe, debased both; these are still good gold, with a fine Christ and the emperor in his jewelled crown, and the tetarteron is the version that turns up most at auction.

obv.english: Jesus Christ

john-ii-aspron-trachy-st-george.note: Alexios I's reform of 1092 made the gold coinage cup-shaped and split it into the pure-gold hyperpyron and this electrum aspron trachy, worth a third of it. John II, 'the Good', the best-loved of the Komnenoi, shares the cross with the soldier saint George. Only two open museum photos so far; more welcome.

carthage-stater-tanit-and-standing-horse.note: Carthage's first full gold coin, struck to pay the mercenary armies it fought with in Sicily. Its Tanit copies the grain-wreathed Persephone of Syracuse's coins, but the calm, upright horse is Carthage's own.

known.detail: Gold half shekel (c. 4.7 g), Tanit / horse before a palm tree, Jenkins & Lewis 52-54.

sources.label: NAC Auction 138 (18 May 2023), lot 111 (4.67 g; Jenkins-Lewis 52-54)
G. K. Jenkins and R. B. Lewis, Carthaginian Gold and Electrum Coins (1963), nos. 52-54

carthage-half-stater-tanit-and-horse-bef.note: The half of the first gold stater, with the palm tree added behind the horse: in Greek the palm and the Phoenicians share one word, phoinix.

carthage-quarter-stater-tanit-and-horse.note: Small change in gold, struck alongside the staters in quarters and fifths, with the same Tanit and horse.
carthage-quarter-stater-tanit-and-horse.search_archive: Cartha AV|gold|oro quarter and fifth stater horse|Pferd

carthage-electrum-trihemistater-tanit-an.note: Struck in pale electrum in the last, hard years of the First Punic War, when Carthage's gold ran short. The winged sun disc with its two cobras is an Egyptian sign the Phoenicians had used for centuries.

carthage-electrum-half-shekel-tanit-and-.note: Electrum of the Second Punic War, struck while Hannibal was in Italy: the old design of the First War came back, on a lighter coin.
carthage-electrum-half-shekel-tanit-and-.search_archive: Cartha EL|electrum|elektron shekel and half shekel horse|Pferd
